title: Jury recommends first-aid training for Vancouver police after coroner's inquest
subtitle: Vancouver Police should ensure CPR and first aid training is mandatory for its officers and jail guards and all jail staff be required to carry out mock medical emergency training to ensure each person knows his role, a coroner's inquest jury recommended on Wednesday. The five-person jury hearing the inquest into the death of Cheryl Ann Cowan, 58, in December 2014 also recommended the force install video cameras in police wagons used to transport prisoners.
article: Vancouver Police should ensure CPR and first aid training is mandatory for its officers and jail guards and all jail staff be required to carry out mock medical emergency training to ensure each person knows his role, a coroner's inquest jury recommended on Wednesday.
The five-person jury hearing the inquest into the death of Cheryl Ann Cowan, 58, in December 2014 also recommended the force install video cameras in police wagons used to transport prisoners.
The jury determined Cowan died from a brain injury from lack of oxygen caused by a heart attack and that hypothermia and chronic alcoholism were contributing factors.

More details were revealed at the three-day inquest into interactions Cowan, a mother of two grown boys who used to teach at the exclusive York House private school but ended up alcoholic and homeless, had with police and factors that likely contributed to her death.

The inquest also heard from other witnesses that it's standard medical procedure for CPR immediately to be administered on an unconscious person without an obvious pulse or who's not breathing except in rare instances.
"If you believe there is no pulse, you should immediately begin CPR unless the body is decomposed or decapitated," testified VPD Insp. John de Haas, who oversees Vancouver jail staff.
De Haas also said he was "shocked" and "quite disturbed" an emergency "code blue," calling all available medical staff to the emergency at the jail on the morning of Dec. 15, 2014, wasn't called.

Testimony heard by and video shown to the inquest showed the jail doctor, two jail nurses, VPD guards, sheriffs and the VPD constable of the wagon failed to immediately start CPR on Cowan, who was discovered slumped over with no vital signs after 48 minutes in the wagon.
She had been arrested and charged with trespassing and other minor charges after her estranged husband found her in his Dunbar house at 6 a.m.

It was a cold evening and she was wearing slippers and pajama bottoms with several layers of clothing, was surrounded by cigarette butts, empty wine bottles and bags of her belongings and was intoxicated. It appeared she had been in the carport all night.
The inquest learned she had a core temperature of 32 degrees Celsius, making her "severely to moderately" hypothermic, which can cause heart problems, Dr. Robert Saunders testified.

He also testified that lack of oxygen to the brain starts to kill brain cells within a minute, in three minutes there is damage, in 10 minutes the damage is irreversible and in 15 minutes it causes death.

It wasn't until paramedics arrived at the Vancouver jail that CPR was started, 11 minutes after Cowan was discovered, according to the Independent Investigations Office timeline in its report clearing the wagon driver of any wrongdoing.

The report also noted the wagon had arrived at the jail 12 minutes before its door was opened by the driver, who according to protocol then (which has since been changed), first delivered Cowan's personal belongings to jail staff.

Saunders said it's not known when Cowan had a heart attack but he speculated it was recent because she was resuscitated quickly when CPR was begun. She however remained on life support until she died eight days later without ever regaining consciousness.

Dr. Samuel Gutman, president of Rockdoc Consulting, which has since Cowan's death entered into a contract to provide medical staff for the Vancouver jail, told the inquest the protocol is that jail doctors and nurses do not declare the death of individuals on the jail grounds.

"We will review and examine the report from the inquest and the recommended changes to any practices, policies and procedures to ensure we are doing everything possible to keep those in our care safe," said VPD spokesman Const. Brian Montague.
